solution:
**(C)** non-polar molecular solid

Molecular solids are the class of crystalline solids whose constituent particles are neutral molecules (§1.3.3), and they are sub-classified by the force that holds those molecules together: a permanent dipole-dipole force gives a polar molecular solid, a London dispersion force gives a non-polar molecular solid, and a hydrogen bond gives a hydrogen bonded molecular solid.

Solid iodine is built of discrete \(\text{I}_{2}\) molecules. The two bonded atoms are identical, so the I-I bond is purely covalent, its bond moment is zero and the molecule carries no permanent dipole. The only force acting between neighbouring \(\text{I}_{2}\) molecules is therefore the weak London dispersion force.

\(\therefore\) Iodine exists as a non-polar molecular solid.

Why the other three fail: an ionic solid is built from cations and anions held by coulomb force (§1.3.1) and iodine contains no ions at all; a polar molecular solid needs a permanent dipole, which a homonuclear diatomic molecule cannot have; a hydrogen bonded molecular solid needs hydrogen bonded to fluorine, oxygen or nitrogen, and there is no hydrogen anywhere in \(\text{I}_{2}\).

The classification agrees with the observed properties of iodine, a soft solid of low melting point that sublimes readily and does not conduct electricity, which is what weak dispersion forces between neutral molecules predict.

stem: An **ionic compound crystallises in FCC type structure** with 'A' ions at the centre of each face and 'B' ions occupying corners of the cube. The formula of compound is ______.
solution:
**(B)** \(\text{A}_{3}\text{B}\)

The unit cell is face centred cubic, so it has ions at its eight corners and at the centre of each of its six faces.

i. 'B' ions occupy the 8 corners. Each corner of a cube is shared by 8 neighbouring cubes, so each corner ion contributes \(\tfrac{1}{8}\) to this cell.

Number of B ions belonging to the unit cell \(= 8 \times \tfrac{1}{8} = 1\)

ii. 'A' ions occupy the centres of the 6 faces. Each face is shared between 2 neighbouring cubes, so each face centre ion contributes \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) to this cell.

Number of A ions belonging to the unit cell \(= 6 \times \tfrac{1}{2} = 3\)

The unit cell therefore contains 3 A ions and 1 B ion, a ratio of \(3 : 1\).

\(\therefore\) Formula of the compound \(= \text{A}_{3}\text{B}\)

Why the other three fail: \(\text{AB}_{3}\) is what the same count gives if A is taken at the corners and B at the face centres, which reverses the positions the question states; \(\text{AB}\) needs equal numbers of the two ions, as in a caesium chloride type cell with one ion at the corners and the other at the body centre; \(\text{A}\text{B}_{2}\) needs a \(1 : 2\) ratio, which neither the corner count nor the face count of a cube can produce.

Check: the two counts add to \(3 + 1 = 4\) ions per cell, which is the number of lattice points in an fcc cell, so no site has been counted twice or missed.

subtopic: Packing of Particles in Crystal Lattice
stem: An **ionic crystal lattice** has \(\text{r}^{+}/\text{r}^{-}\) radius ratio of 0.320, its **coordination number** is ______.
solution:
**(B)** 4

The coordination number of a cation in an ionic crystal is fixed by the radius ratio \(r^{+}/r^{-}\): the cation must be large enough to hold the anions around it apart, and the limiting ratio for each kind of hole follows from the geometry of that hole.

**Tetrahedral hole, coordination number 4.** Four anions sit at alternate corners of a cube of edge \(b\) with the cation at the centre of the cube. At the limiting ratio the anions just touch along a face diagonal:

\(2r^{-} = \sqrt{2}\,b\ \Rightarrow\ r^{-} = \dfrac{b}{\sqrt{2}}\)

and the cation touches an anion along half a body diagonal:

\(r^{+} + r^{-} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}b\)

\(\dfrac{r^{+}}{r^{-}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}\,b/2}{b/\sqrt{2}} - 1 = \dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{2} - 1 = 0.225\)

**Octahedral hole, coordination number 6.** Four anions sit at the corners of a square of side \(a\) with the cation at its centre. At the limiting ratio the anions just touch along a side, \(2r^{-} = a\), while the cation touches them along the diagonal:

\(2(r^{+} + r^{-}) = \sqrt{2}\,a = 2\sqrt{2}\,r^{-}\)

\(\dfrac{r^{+}}{r^{-}} = \sqrt{2} - 1 = 0.414\)

The ratio given is \(0.320\), and \(0.225 < 0.320 < 0.414\). The cation is thus too large to sit in a trigonal hole yet too small to keep six anions from touching one another in an octahedral hole, so it occupies a tetrahedral hole and is surrounded by four anions.

\(\therefore\) The coordination number of the crystal lattice is 4.

Why the other three fail: a coordination number of 3 needs a radius ratio between \(0.155\) and \(0.225\), and \(0.320\) is above that range; 6 needs \(0.414\) to \(0.732\), and at \(0.320\) the six anions of an octahedral arrangement would have to overlap one another; 8, the body centred cubic arrangement of the caesium chloride type, needs \(0.732\) to \(1.000\), far above the value given.

stem: The number of atoms per unit cell of **body centred cubic** is:. \(a\) 1 (b) 2 (d) 4 (d) 6
solution:
A body centred cubic (bcc) unit cell has particles at its eight corners and one particle at the centre of the cube.

**Corner particles.** Each corner of a cube is shared by 8 neighbouring unit cells, so each corner particle contributes \(\tfrac{1}{8}\) to this cell.

Contribution from the corners \(= 8 \times \tfrac{1}{8} = 1\) atom

**Body centre particle.** The particle at the centre of the cube lies wholly inside this cell and is shared with no other cell, so it contributes 1 whole atom.

Contribution from the body centre \(= 1 \times 1 = 1\) atom

\(\therefore\) Number of atoms per bcc unit cell \(= 1 + 1 = 2\)

Check: taking \(z = 2\) with the bcc contact condition \(4r = \sqrt{3}\,a\), that is \(r = 0.433\,a\), the packing efficiency comes out as

\(\dfrac{2 \times \tfrac{4}{3}\pi (0.433a)^{3}}{a^{3}} = 0.68\)

the 68 % established for the bcc lattice, so the count of 2 atoms per cell is consistent.

subtopic: Packing of Particles in Crystal Lattice
stem: The **co-ordination number** of atoms in **body centred cubic** structure (bcc) is ______.
solution:
**(B)** 8

The coordination number of a particle is the number of its nearest neighbours, that is the number of particles it touches.

In a body centred cubic lattice the corner particles do not touch one another; contact runs along the body diagonal, through the particle at the centre of the cube, so that

\(4r = \sqrt{3}\,a\)

The distance from the body centre to any corner is half the body diagonal, \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}a = 2r\), which is exactly the centre-to-centre distance of two touching spheres. The body centre particle therefore touches all 8 corner particles of its cube, four in the layer below it and four in the layer above.

Each corner particle is itself the body centre of one of the eight cubes meeting at that corner, so it too has 8 nearest neighbours.

\(\therefore\) The coordination number of atoms in a bcc structure is 8.

Why the other three fail: 6 is the coordination number of the simple cubic lattice, where a particle touches four neighbours in its own layer, one above and one below; 4 is the number of particles in an fcc unit cell and the coordination number of two-dimensional square close packing, neither of which is the quantity asked for; 12 is the coordination number of the hcp and ccp lattices, in which each sphere touches six neighbours in its own layer and three in each of the layers above and below.

stem: The relation between radius of sphere and edge length in **body centered cubic lattice** is given by formula:.
solution:
**(C)** \(\text{r} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\text{a}\)

In a body centred cubic cell the corner spheres do not touch one another. Contact runs along the body diagonal, through the sphere at the centre of the cube.

A cube of edge \(a\) has a body diagonal of length \(\sqrt{3}\,a\). Reading along that diagonal, it is made up of the radius of one corner sphere, the whole diameter of the body centre sphere and the radius of the opposite corner sphere:

\(\sqrt{3}\,a = r + 2r + r = 4r\)

\(\therefore\ r = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a = 0.433\,a\)

Why the other three fail: \(3r = 4a\) rearranges to \(r = 1.33\,a\), a sphere of radius greater than the whole edge of the cell it has to sit inside, which is impossible; \(r = 3\,a \times 4\) is larger still and is not the relation for any lattice; \(r = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{4}a\) is the face centred cubic relation, obtained from the face diagonal \(4r = \sqrt{2}\,a\), and in a bcc cell the centre of a face is empty so no contact runs along a face diagonal at all.

Check: \(2r = 0.866\,a < a\), so two corner spheres along an edge do not overlap; and substituting \(r = 0.433\,a\) with \(z = 2\) gives a packing efficiency of \(\dfrac{2 \times \tfrac{4}{3}\pi (0.433a)^{3}}{a^{3}} = 0.68\), the 68 % established for the bcc lattice.

stem: The number of particles present in **Face Centred Cubic Unit Cell** is/are ______.
solution:
**(D)** 4

A face centred cubic unit cell has particles at its eight corners and at the centre of each of its six faces.

**Corner particles.** Each corner of a cube is shared by 8 neighbouring cubes, so each corner particle contributes \(\tfrac{1}{8}\) to this cell.

Contribution from the corners \(= 8 \times \tfrac{1}{8} = 1\) particle

**Face centre particles.** Each face is shared between 2 neighbouring cubes, so each face centre particle contributes \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) to this cell.

Contribution from the faces \(= 6 \times \tfrac{1}{2} = 3\) particles

\(\therefore\) Number of particles in an fcc unit cell \(= 1 + 3 = 4\)

Why the other three fail: 1 is the number of particles in a simple cubic unit cell, which carries particles at its corners only; 2 is the number in a body centred cubic unit cell, one from the corners together with the one at the body centre; 3 is the contribution of the six face centres by itself, that is the count made with the corner contribution left out.

Check: taking \(z = 4\) with the fcc contact condition \(4r = \sqrt{2}\,a\), that is \(r = 0.3535\,a\), the packing efficiency comes out as \(\dfrac{4 \times \tfrac{4}{3}\pi (0.3535a)^{3}}{a^{3}} = 0.74\), the 74 % established for the ccp or fcc lattice, so the count of 4 particles per cell is consistent.

stem: To prepare **n-type semiconductor**, the impurity to be added to silicon should have the following number of valence electrons?.
solution:
**(D)** 5

Silicon belongs to group 14 and has four valence electrons. In the silicon crystal all four are used in covalent bonds with its four neighbours, so there is no free electron left to carry a current.

An n-type semiconductor is obtained by adding to the group 14 element a group 15 element such as P, As, Sb or Bi (§1.9.5), and a group 15 atom has **five** valence electrons. When such an atom takes the place of a silicon atom in the lattice, four of its five valence electrons form the four covalent bonds with the surrounding silicon atoms and the fifth electron is left over. That electron is held in no bond, so it is free to move through the crystal and conduct.

Conduction is therefore by extra negative carriers, which is what the n in n-type stands for.

\(\therefore\) The impurity added to silicon must have 5 valence electrons.

Why the other three fail: an impurity with 3 valence electrons is a group 13 element such as B, Ga or In, which leaves one covalent bond one electron short and creates a hole, giving a p-type semiconductor instead; an impurity with 4 valence electrons brings exactly as many electrons as the silicon atom it replaces, so neither a spare electron nor a hole is produced and the solid remains an intrinsic semiconductor; an impurity with 1 valence electron is an alkali metal, which is not among the dopants used here and cannot take up a four-bonded site in a covalent lattice.

**(D)** \(\text{NiO}\)

A Schottky defect is a **stoichiometric** point defect: equal numbers of cations and anions are missing from their regular lattice sites, so the density of the crystal falls while its composition and its electrical neutrality are both unchanged (§1.8.1 iii). It forms in ionic crystals whose cation and anion are of nearly the same size and whose coordination number is high, and \(\text{NaCl}\), \(\text{KCl}\) and \(\text{AgBr}\) are the crystals named in the chapter as showing it.

\(\text{NiO}\) is not such a crystal. It shows a **metal deficiency** defect, which is non-stoichiometric: some \(\text{Ni}^{2+}\) sites are vacant, and electrical neutrality is restored not by an equal number of oxide ions going missing but by an equal amount of positive charge appearing as \(\text{Ni}^{3+}\) on neighbouring nickel sites. The solid that results is metal deficient, of composition \(\text{Ni}_{1-x}\text{O}\), so the ratio of the two kinds of ion no longer matches the formula, which is exactly what a Schottky defect does not do.

\(\therefore\) Schottky defect is not observed in \(\text{NiO}\).

Why the other three fail: \(\text{NaCl}\) and \(\text{KCl}\) are built of singly charged ions of comparable size in a lattice of coordination number 6, the very conditions the Schottky defect requires, and both are quoted in the chapter as showing it; \(\text{AgBr}\) is the crystal usually cited as showing the Schottky and the Frenkel defect together, so it too shows the Schottky defect.
